searches.note: One of the thirty one returned nothing of use (its terms too many, on Gilette); two on the Yquem domain (the soils, the years 1964 to 1974) returned little until a third settled the years. No WebFetch was tried. Seven searches of the share are left unspent.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all (the run's shared allowance was spent), resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and owners and their years, the rank, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (yquem.fr, chateaucoutet.com, suduiraut.com, the Suduiraut sheets on a merchant's host), the appellation body (the INAO), the Union des Grands Crus de Bordeaux for the estate's own sheet, or a primary record (Jefferson's letters in Founders Online).

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (The Wine Cellar Insider, The Wine Doctor, Wine with Seth, a critic's pages) was read as a lead and never cited.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price (costly barrels in the Gilette story became oak barrels), no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative (top in a label line became leading), no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. The lint's notes on the most concentrated grapes are the estate of Coutet's own words for its pick, a primary source, and stand; still stands, of a medieval tower, will not age.

tested: The tenure of 1593 and full ownership in 1711 (the estate's history page, Wikipedia, read through search): confirmed, the first as the estate's feudal tenure; founded stays empty.
The marriage of 1785 and the widowhood three years later (Wikipedia, a second account giving 1788): confirmed; through the Revolution was found in neither and is cut.

Jefferson's orders (his letter to Bondfield of 18 December 1787 naming his letter to Yquem of that day, Lur-Saluces's reply of 7 January 1788, his letter to Fenwick of 6 September 1790 ordering thirty dozen of Sauterne for the President and ten for himself): confirmed from the letters; the Washington story is now told as fact.
The rank of 1855: the library and the Codex: stands.
The years with no Yquem: the estate's 2012 page names 1910, 1915, 1930, 1951, 1952, 1964, 1972, 1974 and 1992 and adds 2012; confirmed, 1964 included.

The making: new barrels and twenty months in the ageing cellar (the estate's expertise page); successive rounds of picking (its vintage pages): confirmed; the blend of 2022 and 2023, four fifths and seven tenths Sémillon, keeps about three quarters.
The soils: the estate's 1994 vintage note on sandy and clayey plots; gravel found in no result and cut. One search of the estate's domain for the soils returned nothing more.
LVMH: relatives sold 55 per cent in 1996, a court forced the head of the family to sell in 1999 and LVMH took control (Wine Spectator, Decanter, CNN Money): the story corrected.
Y first made in 1959 (the estate's Y 1959 page, a merchant's listing, Wikipedia): confirmed.

The rules: nobody living named (the head of the family until 2004, who died at 89 by one account, and the director who followed him stay unnamed), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash; the questions have one key each and explanations that name the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: In 1593 the Sauvage family, local nobles, took the tenure of Yquem, and over the next two centuries they made the hill above Sauternes their own. In 1785 the Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family; widowed three years later, she ran the estate herself through the Revolution. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), touring Bordeaux as the American minister in Paris, ordered Yquem for himself and, the story goes, for George Washington. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers set Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, a rank made for it and never shared. The Lur-Saluces family kept the estate for more than two centuries and kept its discipline: many passes through the vines for each harvest, and no wine at all under the name in years judged too poor, among them 1964, 1972, 1974 and 1992. In 1959 they added a dry white, Y, sold as Bordeaux. After a long family dispute the estate passed in 1999 to the luxury group LVMH, and Yquem again declined a vintage in 2012. Guests ask for it by name, and it needs no partner at all, though foie gras and Roquefort are its classic companions.
changed.now: In 1593 a member of the Sauvage family, local nobles, was given the feudal tenure of Yquem, as the estate tells it, and in 1711 the family became its full owners. In 1785 the Sauvage heiress married into the Lur-Saluces family; widowed three years later, she ran the estate herself. In December 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), the American minister in Paris, ordered Yquem for himself, and in 1790 he ordered thirty dozen bottles more from the estate for President George Washington (1732 to 1799). In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers set Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, above the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, a rank made for it and never shared. The family kept its discipline: many passes through the vines at each harvest, and no wine at all under the name in years judged too poor, nine of them in the twentieth century, from 1910 to 1992. In 1959 it added a dry white, Y, sold as Bordeaux. In 1996 relatives sold a majority to the luxury group LVMH, which took control in 1999 after a court battle with the head of the family, and in 2012 Yquem again declined a vintage. For a sommelier it is the clearest lesson in what Sauternes asks: noble rot, patience and the nerve to sell nothing in a poor year.
changed.why: The estate gives the feudal tenure of 1593 and full ownership in 1711; Jefferson's letters give the order of December 1787 and thirty dozen bottles of Sauternes for the President in 1790; the estate lists the nine years with no wine; relatives sold LVMH a majority in 1996 and a court ruling gave it control in 1999; the close on foie gras and Roquefort was a pairing with no source.

changed.was: Climens lies on the Barsac plateau, where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and the autumn mists that follow bring noble rot to the grapes. Barsac's soils are thin over limestone, and its wines are known for tension rather than weight; Climens, on the commune's higher ground of red sand, became the clearest example. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked it among the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, beneath Yquem alone. In 1971 it was bought by a Bordeaux family that already held several growths of the Médoc, and from 1992 a daughter of that family ran it for some thirty years. She kept the vineyard to Sémillon alone, picked in many passes, and kept each pass and each parcel apart in barrel until a late blend, so that the freshness of the finished wine was chosen rather than left to chance; in the 2010s she turned the farming to biodynamics. In 2022 the family sold the estate. Through each change of hands Climens has held to one idea: that Barsac's limestone and Sémillon alone can make a sweet wine that feels weightless. Its lesson for a candidate is simple: Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac, never required.
changed.now: Climens lies on the Barsac plateau, where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and the autumn mists that follow bring noble rot to the grapes. The Gounouilhou family of Bordeaux held it for decades after, until 1971, when it was bought by another Bordeaux family that already held growths of the Médoc. From 1992 a daughter of that family ran it. She kept the vineyard to Sémillon alone, picked in many passes, and kept each pass and each parcel apart in barrel until a late blend, and in the 2010s she turned the farming to biodynamics. In 2022 the family sold a majority of the estate to new owners. Through each change of hands Climens has held to one idea: that Barsac's limestone and Sémillon alone can make a sweet wine that feels weightless. Its lesson for a candidate is simple: Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac, never required.

changed.was: Aquitaine belonged to the English crown when the square tower at the heart of Coutet was raised in the thirteenth century, and the estate grew around it on the Barsac plateau. From the late eighteenth century Coutet belonged to the Lur-Saluces family, who also held Yquem, and it stayed with them for well over a hundred years. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Coutet a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac, beside its neighbour Climens, the two Barsac estates of that rank. In the twentieth century it passed through other hands, and its rare selection, Cuvée Madame, from the ripest Sémillon of exceptional years, made the estate's name among collectors. In 1977 the Baly family bought Coutet and set about restoring the vineyard, the cellars and the old buildings. They kept the Barsac style that the plateau gives: sweet wine with the tension of limestone, less broad than the Sauternes of the hills, and in the years of plenty they set aside the few barrels of Cuvée Madame. Coutet makes the case for Barsac's own appellation, and for the right of a Barsac estate to print Sauternes instead if it wishes.
changed.now: Coutet began as a fortress while Aquitaine belonged to the English crown, in the thirteenth century by the estate's account, and its square, battlemented tower still stands in the courtyard. Confiscated by the state in 1794, it later passed by inheritance to a Lur-Saluces, of the family that held Yquem. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Coutet a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac, beside Climens, the two Barsac estates of that rank. The Lur-Saluces kept it until the early 1920s, when it passed to the family of a Lyon industrialist, and a lady of that family owned it until 1977. In her honour, as the estate tells it, the vineyard workers gave her a day's work at harvest, picking the most concentrated grapes of the two oldest Sémillon parcels, and from 1943 that pick became Cuvée Madame, made only in rare years. In 1977 the Baly family bought Coutet and kept the tradition. Coutet makes the case for Barsac's own appellation: sweet wine with the tension of limestone, less broad than the Sauternes of the hills, and the right of a Barsac estate to print Sauternes instead if it wishes.
changed.why: The estate gives the fortress of the thirteenth century, the confiscation of 1794, the inheritance by a Lur-Saluces, their tenure until the 1920s, the lady owner from 1922 to 1977, the day's work in her honour and the first Cuvée Madame of 1943; Wikipedia and merchants give the Baly purchase of 1977; from the late eighteenth century and the collectors line were unsourced.

changed.was: Formal gardens in the French manner, attributed by tradition to André Le Nôtre (1613 to 1700), the gardener of Versailles, frame the house at Suduiraut. The estate carries the name of the Suduiraut family, its owners in the seventeenth century, whose house, the story goes, was burnt during the Fronde, the civil wars of the 1650s, and rebuilt in the decades after. The vineyard climbs the low hills of Preignac to the border of Yquem, and the Ciron's mists that settle there bring noble rot in most autumns. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Suduiraut a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac. Through the twentieth century it passed between private owners until 1992, when it was bought by AXA Millésimes, the wine estates of the French insurance group, which had taken Pichon Baron in Pauillac in 1987. The new owners kept the house style, broad Sémillon picked late in many passes, and added a dry white under the letter S, as Rieussec has its R and Guiraud its G, so that sound grapes from years with little rot find a use. Set beside Climens or Coutet, Suduiraut gives the other face of the district: Preignac's breadth against the tension of Barsac across the Ciron.
changed.now: In 1580 a marriage brought this Preignac estate to the Suduiraut family, whose name it carries. During the Fronde, the civil wars of 1648 to 1653, the old manor was plundered and burnt, and in 1670 a grandson of that marriage built a new château, framed by formal gardens in the French manner attributed to André Le Nôtre (1613 to 1700), the gardener of Versailles, or to his workshop. In the eighteenth century it passed to a nephew, and for a time, by the estate's account, its wine was sold as Cru du Roy. The vineyard runs to the border of Yquem, and the Ciron's mists that settle there bring noble rot in most autumns. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Suduiraut a Premier Cru of Sauternes and Barsac. It stayed in private hands until 1992, when it was bought by AXA Millésimes, the wine estates of the French insurance group, whose first purchase had been Pichon Baron in Pauillac in 1987. The new owners kept the house style, broad Sémillon picked late in many passes, and from 2004 made a dry white of the old vines, S de Suduiraut, sold as Bordeaux. Set beside Climens or Coutet, Suduiraut gives the other face of the district: Preignac's breadth against the tension of Barsac across the Ciron.

changed.was: When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification of the sweet wines in 1855, Gilette, in Preignac, one of the five communes of Sauternes, was not among the estates ranked, and since that list has never been reopened it has stayed outside it. The appellation decree of 1936 gave it the same Sauternes name as Yquem, and what has made Gilette known is not rank but time. For generations the estate was worked by the Médeville family, growers of Preignac, and their way of raising the wine is what sets it apart. After fermentation the wine goes not into barrels but into small concrete vats, filled to the brim so that little air reaches it, and there it rests for many years, often close to twenty, before it is bottled. It then waits again in the cellar, so that a Gilette reaches a list already decades old. The great years become Crème de Tête; lesser years are bottled under plainer labels. The result is a Sauternes aged without oak and without the breath of a barrel: deep and mellow, yet with a freshness that surprises a guest who reads the vintage. For a sommelier it is the rare chance to offer mature Sauternes without a cellar of one's own.
changed.now: When the Bordeaux brokers ranked the sweet wines in 1855, Gilette, in Preignac, one of the five communes of Sauternes, was not among the estates listed, and since that list has never been reopened it has stayed outside it. The decree of 30 September 1936 that first recognised the Sauternes appellation gave it the same name as Yquem, and what has made Gilette known is not rank but time. For generations the estate has been in the hands of the Médeville family, growers of Preignac. In the 1930s, as the family tells it, the Depression left Bordeaux in a slump, and the family built concrete vats in place of oak barrels. The wine aged there more slowly than in wood, and the family has kept its sweet wine in concrete ever since, often for fifteen to twenty years before bottling, so that a Gilette reaches a list already decades old. Its leading selection is bottled as Crème de Tête. The result is a Sauternes aged without oak: deep and mellow, yet with a freshness that surprises a guest who reads the vintage. For a sommelier it is the rare chance to offer mature Sauternes without a cellar of one's own.
changed.why: The INAO's rules give the decree of 30 September 1936 that first recognised the appellation; Vinfolio and the importer tell the Depression story of the concrete vats as the family's; lesser years under plainer labels and the brimming vats were unsourced.
